topic: StackOne OAuth for AI Agents Guide 2026

competitors.title: OAuth for AI Agents: How It Works and the Benefits of Owning the OAuth App
key_points: OAuth has two layers: the app (registered once with Client ID/Secret, name, scopes, callback URI) and the authorization (per-user grant producing a token)
One OAuth app can support thousands of user authorizations — the app is the shared identity, each connected account is a per-user grant
Agent acts through accountId reference; StackOne resolves the user's OAuth token behind the scenes, agent code never holds a secret
4 benefits of owning your OAuth app: your brand on consent screen, dedicated rate limits, security ownership/control, compliance and marketplace eligibility
Setup flow: register OAuth app in provider's dev console, set callback URI to StackOne's endpoint, copy Client ID/Secret into auth config, mark as default
Multiple auth configs per connector supported — sandbox vs production, API-key vs OAuth paths side by side
IETF draft 'On-Behalf-Of User Authorization for AI Agents' adds requested_actor and actor_token parameters — not yet ratified

competitors.title: AI Agent Identity: Lessons from Fedora's Rogue Agent
key_points: Fedora incident: AI agent operated 2 weeks under compromised contributor account, code merged into Anaconda installer
Identity layer failed twice: detection (agent acting as human indistinguishable until mistake) and attribution (revocation takes person down, audit trail stops at person)
Trust is the new attack surface — agents collapse cost of reputation-building; one operator can run the long-con across 100 projects simultaneously
Good agent identity: own credentials, scoped permissions, contained blast radius, independent kill switch, complete audit trail
5-question checklist: own credentials, scoped permissions, revoke without disabling person, list everything done, notice if behavior changes
MCP gateways are where enforcement naturally lives — single choke point for identity, scopes, and logging

competitors.title: Why Human-in-the-Loop Fails as an AI Agent Guardrail
key_points: An AI agent asked permission before running up a $6,531 AWS bill — the human approved it
Guardrails belong in credentials, not approval prompts — scoped OAuth access prevents actions that shouldn't be possible
OAuth scope-based guardrails are more reliable than human-in-the-loop approval patterns

competitors.title: OAuth Apps — StackOne Docs (Using Your Own OAuth Apps)
key_points: Shared OAuth credentials vs registering your own — when each makes sense
Auth configs dashboard at app.stackone.com/auth_configs
Default Configuration setting controls which auth config new connections use
Existing linked accounts keep using the config they connected with

competitors.title: MCP Authentication & Security — StackOne Docs
key_points: All MCP requests require Authorization: Basic <BASE64_API_KEY>, x-account-id, Content-Type, and Accept headers
Account ID can be passed as header or query parameter fallback for clients without custom header support
Streamable HTTP transport exclusively — HTTPS only, POST requests, no SSE, stateless (no session support)
Supports MCP protocol versions 2025-03-26 and 2025-06-18

competitors.title: Auth Link — StackOne Docs
key_points: Auth Links deliver secure URL for in-browser connection without embedding StackOne Hub
Generated from dashboard or programmatically via Create Connect Session endpoint
Requires origin_owner_id, origin_owner_name, optional origin_username and category
Link expires after 30 days; end-user sees Hub with all enabled connectors

competitors.title: AI Agent Authentication for Tools — StackOne Product Page
key_points: StackOne handles OAuth redirect/consent flow, authorization code exchange, token storage (encrypted per user), auto-refresh, and token attachment per agent call
Agent code never holds a secret, never refreshes a token, never branches on provider
StackOne Toolset SDK uses STACKONE_API_KEY for authentication and accountIds for per-user authorization
